15695:
Chemosh was the national god of Moab, the kingdom east of the Dead Sea. The Moabites were 'the people of Chemosh' just as Israel was the people of Yahweh.

Chemosh is the one neighbouring god whose own worshippers' voice we can still hear clearly, thanks to the Mesha Stele, an inscription of about 840 BC in which King Mesha of Moab explains his country's history in exactly the terms the book of Kings uses for Israel: his god was angry and let the enemy oppress the land, then his god said 'Go!' and gave him victory.
15696: No narrative myth survives. The Mesha Stele gives Chemosh's theology: Omri king of Israel humbled Moab for many days 'because Chemosh was angry with his land'. Then Chemosh restored the land in Mesha's days. Chemosh told Mesha, 'Go, take Nebo from Israel', and Mesha killed its 7,000 inhabitants because he had devoted them (the same idea as the Hebrew herem, 'devotion to destruction') to Ashtar-Chemosh. He took the vessels of Yahweh from Nebo and dragged them before Chemosh. Chemosh 'drove out' the king of Israel before him.
15697:
Israel's songs taunt Moab as 'the people of Chemosh' whose sons and daughters became fugitives (Num 21:29; Jer 48:46). Jephthah tells the Ammonite king, 'Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you?', treating Chemosh as Ammon's god, either a slip, a sign that Ammon then ruled Moabite land, or a rhetorical move (Judg 11:24). Solomon built a high place for 'Chemosh the abomination of Moab' east of Jerusalem (1 Kgs 11:7); Josiah defiled it (2 Kgs 23:13). Jeremiah says Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and princes (Jer 48:7; Jer 48:13).

The most startling text is 2 Kgs 3. Mesha, king of Moab, a sheep-breeder who paid Israel huge tribute, rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 3:4-5). Israel, Judah and Edom invaded and besieged him at Kir-hareseth. In desperation Mesha offered his eldest son as a burnt offering on the wall, 'and there came great wrath against Israel', and they withdrew (2 Kgs 3:26-27). Whose wrath? Readings include: (1) Chemosh's wrath, the writer admitting the foreign god's power in his own land (a minority view); (2) Yahweh's wrath against Israel for some fault or for provoking the act; (3) human fury or horror, the Moabites' rage or Israel's own dismay, sapping their will; (4) the writer deliberately leaves it unexplained. The text does not say.

Rimmon was the storm god of Damascus, capital of Aram (Syria): the same Hadad that Canaanites called Baal, under his Akkadian title Ramman, 'the Thunderer'. Several Aramean kings carried his name: Ben-Hadad ('son of Hadad'), Hadadezer ('Hadad is help') and Tabrimmon ('Rimmon is good').

He appears in one of the Bible's most human scenes. Naaman, the Syrian general healed of skin disease by Elisha, promises to worship only Israel's God, but asks forgiveness in advance for when his king leans on his arm and he must bow with him in the house of Rimmon. Elisha simply says, 'Go in peace.'
15734: Hadad of Damascus was the Aramean storm god and divine king, in the same tradition as Baal of Ugarit and Adad of Assyria. Kings of Aram claimed he went before them in battle, as the Tel Dan inscription says of Hazael. The Akkadian epithet Ramman ('thunderer') became the Hebrew Rimmon, which also happens to be the ordinary word for 'pomegranate'.
15735:
Naaman asks for two mule-loads of Israelite earth so he can worship Yahweh in Damascus, a sign that he still thinks of gods as tied to their land. He also asks pardon for bowing with his king in the house of Rimmon, and Elisha replies, 'Go in peace' (2 Kgs 5:17-19). Christians have long debated whether this was a concession to weakness, tolerance of outward conformity, or simply a blessing on his departure without approving the request.

Ahaz copies the design of an altar he saw in Damascus and installs it in Yahweh's temple, sacrificing 'to the gods of Damascus that had struck him' (2 Kgs 16:10-16; 2 Chr 28:23). Zechariah speaks of a great mourning in Jerusalem 'like the mourning for Hadad-rimmon in the valley of Megiddo' (Zech 12:11). This may be ritual weeping for a dying storm god, or a place-name commemorating the mourning for King Josiah, killed at Megiddo; it is debated.

15774:
Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi) was a shepherd god, husband of the love goddess Inanna (Ishtar). In Mesopotamian myth he was dragged down to the underworld, and each summer women mourned him with laments as the green pastures withered.

The Bible mentions him once. In a vision dated about 592 BC, Ezekiel is taken to the north gate of the Jerusalem temple and sees 'women sitting, weeping for Tammuz' (Ezek 8:14). The month of Tammuz still has his name in the Jewish calendar.
15775:
In the Sumerian 'Descent of Inanna', Inanna goes down to the underworld, dies there, and is revived on condition that she sends someone in her place. Returning, she finds her husband Dumuzi enthroned and unmoved by her absence, and hands him to the demons. Dumuzi's sister Geshtinanna mourns him and agrees to share his fate: each spends half the year below. (This ending was understood only in the 1960s; earlier scholars thought he simply stayed dead.) Many other Sumerian songs tell of the courtship of Inanna and Dumuzi and of laments for the slain shepherd.

Sir James Frazer's *The Golden Bough* (1890 onward) grouped Tammuz with Adonis, Osiris and Attis as 'dying and rising gods'. Later scholars, notably Jonathan Z. Smith, criticised that category as forced; others, such as Tryggve Mettinger, defend a modified version of it. It is a live debate.
15776:
Ezekiel's temple vision (Ezek 8) is a tour of four 'abominations', each worse than the last: an 'image of jealousy' at the north gate; seventy elders burning incense to drawings of creeping things and beasts; women weeping for Tammuz at the north gate of the temple; and twenty-five men with their backs to the temple, bowing east to the sun (Ezek 8:14-16). The point is that even in Jerusalem's last years before 586 BC, Judahites were mourning a Mesopotamian god at Yahweh's own house.

Some scholars suggest other veiled references: Isaiah's 'pleasant plants' or 'gardens of Adonis' planted for a foreign god (Isa 17:10-11), and Daniel's 'the one beloved by women' (Dan 11:37). These are speculative.
15778: At the north gate of the temple Ezekiel sees women mourning Tammuz, and is told he will see still greater abominations.

Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) has 'Thammuz', whose yearly wound turned the river Adonis red and moved the daughters of Zion to the lament Ezekiel saw. The Jewish month and the Arabic Syrian month Tammuz still carry his name.

15807:
The 'Queen of Heaven' was a goddess worshipped by ordinary Judean families in Jeremiah's day, around 600 BC. Children gathered wood, fathers lit the fire, and women kneaded dough to bake cakes for her (Jer 7:18).

Jeremiah 44 gives one of the most revealing exchanges in the Bible. After Jerusalem fell, Judean refugees in Egypt told Jeremiah flatly that they would keep burning incense to the Queen of Heaven, because when they did, they had plenty of bread and were well, and since they stopped (under Josiah's reform) they had lacked everything. From their point of view, abandoning the goddess was what caused the disaster. Who exactly she was is not certain.
15808: Her worshippers did not leave us her stories under this title. If she was Ishtar, her myths include the descent to the underworld and her love for Tammuz; if Astarte, she was the Phoenician queen goddess of love and war; if Anat, Egyptian texts call Anat 'lady of heaven'. What the Bible does record is her worshippers' theology: a household goddess who repays faithful offerings with food, health and safety.
15809:
Jeremiah condemns the family cult of the Queen of Heaven in Jerusalem (Jer 7:16-20). Later, in Pathros in Upper Egypt, the women say their husbands knew and approved of their incense, drink offerings and cakes 'made in her image' (Jer 44:15-19). The men and women together vow to continue. Jeremiah replies that it was exactly this incense that God remembered and punished, and announces that Pharaoh Hophra will fall (Jer 44:20-30).

The identity of the Queen is debated. (1) Ishtar: 'Queen of Heaven' is a standard Akkadian title of Ishtar (sharrat shame), and the cakes recall Mesopotamian kamanu cakes offered to Ishtar; kawwanim is probably a loanword from that term. (2) Astarte: the western form of Ishtar, popular in the Levant and Egypt. (3) Anat. (4) Asherah. Many scholars (e.g. Susan Ackerman) argue she was a blend of Ishtar and Astarte. All agree she was a goddess of popular, family religion, and that women played the leading role in her cult.

15843:
Baal Hammon and Tanit were the chief gods of Carthage, the Phoenician colony in North Africa founded from Tyre. They are not in the Bible. They are here because the Carthage 'tophet', a sacred area full of urns of burned babies and young animals dedicated to them, is the main archaeological evidence used to understand the biblical Topheth and the cult of Molech.

Whether the Carthaginians routinely sacrificed their children, as Greek and Roman writers said, or whether the tophet was a special cemetery for infants who died naturally, is one of the most heated debates in Mediterranean archaeology.
15844: Few Punic myths survive. Baal Hammon was the senior god, often shown as a bearded elder on a throne flanked by sphinxes; the Greeks equated him with Kronos and the Romans with Saturn. The meaning of 'Hammon' is debated: 'lord of the incense altar' (compare the Hebrew hammanim, incense altars, in Lev 26:30 and Isa 17:8), or 'lord of Mount Amanus' in Syria. Tanit, called 'face of Baal', rose to prominence in Carthage from the 5th century BC and was later worshipped as Juno Caelestis. Inscriptions on the tophet stelae follow a set formula: 'To the Lady Tanit, face of Baal, and to the Lord Baal Hammon, what X son of Y vowed, because he heard his voice.'
15845: Neither god is named in the Bible. The connection is through practice. The Bible describes a 'Topheth' in the Hinnom valley where children were burned (Jer 7:31; 2 Kgs 23:10), calls the practice making children 'pass through the fire' (Deut 18:10; 2 Kgs 16:3), and says Phoenician-influenced kings brought foreign customs into Israel (1 Kgs 16:31). Scholars borrowed the biblical word 'tophet' for the Punic sanctuaries. Carthage's Punic inscriptions also use mlk as a sacrifice term, which led Otto Eissfeldt to his theory about Molech. The Bible's own word hammanim, incense altars that God threatens to destroy, may share a root with Baal Hammon's name (Lev 26:30; 2 Chr 34:4), though this is uncertain.
15847: The biblical Topheth, where children were burned, gave its name to the Punic sanctuaries.
15849: Deuteronomy condemns burning sons and daughters as something the nations do for their gods.
15851: A rare word for incense altars that may be related to the name Baal Hammon (uncertain).
15852: discovered 1921 (F. Icard and P. Gielly); excavated 1920s-1940s and 1976-1979 (Lawrence Stager)
15853: A sacred precinct used from about the 8th century BC until Rome destroyed Carthage in 146 BC, with layer upon layer of urns holding the burned bones of infants, young children and young animals (lambs, kids), under stone markers and inscribed stelae to Tanit and Baal Hammon. Stager estimated about 20,000 urns were deposited between c. 400 and 200 BC alone. Similar tophets exist in Sicily (Motya), Sardinia (Tharros, Sulcis) and Malta.
15856: Jeffrey Schwartz and colleagues (*PLoS ONE*, 2010) found that many of the infants were prenatal or perinatal and argued the tophet was a cemetery for babies who died naturally. Patricia Smith, Lawrence Stager and colleagues (*Antiquity*, 2011 and 2013), correcting for shrinkage of burned bone, found that the ages cluster at one to two months after birth, which fits a pattern of sacrifice rather than natural mortality. Other specialists (e.g. Paolo Xella and colleagues, *Antiquity* 2013) argue the inscriptions, which speak of vows and offerings, plus the classical sources, point to sacrifice. The question is still debated, though many specialists now accept that at least some infants were sacrificed.

15860: Diodorus Siculus (*Library* 20.14) says that in 310 BC, besieged by Agathocles, Carthage sacrificed some 200-500 children of noble families to Kronos, whose bronze statue had outstretched hands from which the child rolled into a pit of fire. Plutarch (*On Superstition* 13) describes drums and flutes drowning the cries. Tertullian (*Apology* 9) says children were sacrificed to Saturn in Africa into Roman times. These writers were Carthage's enemies or outsiders, so their reliability is part of the debate.
